questions.stem: Economic activity is best defined as:
options: the total amount of money held by all households and businesses
the buying and selling of company shares on the stock exchange
the spending by government on public services such as health and education
the production, distribution and consumption of goods and services
questions.explanation: Economic activity covers everything involved in producing, distributing and consuming goods and services to satisfy needs and wants. Share trading and government spending are parts of it, not the whole.

questions.stem: Material living standards refer to:
options: the quality of the natural environment in which people live
the quantity and quality of goods and services people can access
the health, safety and freedom that people enjoy in their daily lives
the level of happiness that people report in wellbeing surveys
questions.explanation: Material living standards concern the tangible goods and services people can buy and use, usually measured by income or output per person. Health, freedom and the environment are aspects of non-material living standards.

questions.stem: Which indicator is best suited to measuring non-material living standards?
options: average life expectancy at birth
real GDP per capita
average household disposable income
the number of cars per 1,000 people
questions.explanation: Life expectancy reflects health, one of the qualitative parts of wellbeing that make up non-material living standards. Income, output per person and car ownership all measure material living standards.

questions.stem: A city's new factories raise average incomes but increase air pollution and commuting times. The best description of the effect on living standards is that:
options: both material and non-material living standards rise as average incomes increase
material living standards fall while non-material living standards rise
living standards rise overall, because real incomes are now higher
material living standards rise while non-material living standards may fall
questions.explanation: Higher incomes let residents buy more goods and services, raising material living standards, but dirtier air and longer commutes harm health and leisure time. Higher incomes alone do not show that overall living standards rose, because the non-material losses may outweigh them.

questions.stem: The five sectors of the five-sector circular flow model are households, businesses, government and:
options: the financial sector and the overseas sector
the public sector and the private sector
the labour market and the share market
the primary industry sector and the tertiary sector
questions.explanation: The five-sector model adds the financial sector, which channels saving into investment, and the overseas sector, which trades exports and imports, to the three-sector model. The public and private sectors describe ownership, not the model's sectors.

questions.stem: In the five-sector circular flow model, the leakages from the flow of income are:
options: saving, taxation and imports
investment, government spending and exports
saving, investment and exports
consumption, taxation and imports
questions.explanation: Saving, taxation and imports are income that households and businesses do not spend on local production, so they leave the flow. Investment, government spending and exports are the matching injections.

questions.stem: Which is an injection into Australia's circular flow of income?
options: a company paying company tax to the federal government
a Victorian winery's sales of wine to buyers in Japan
a household's purchase of a car made in South Korea
a worker depositing part of her wage in a savings account
questions.explanation: Exports bring spending from overseas into Australian businesses, an injection. Buying an imported car, saving and paying tax all take income out of the flow, so they are leakages.

questions.stem: In a period, injections into the circular flow total $500 billion and leakages total $480 billion. The level of economic activity is likely to:
options: fall, as $480 billion of income is withdrawn from the flow
rise, as more is being added to the flow than is withdrawn
fall, as more is being added to the flow than is withdrawn
stay constant, as injections and leakages always balance
questions.explanation: When injections exceed leakages, spending in the economy grows, so production, income and employment rise. Injections and leakages are equal only when the economy is in equilibrium, which is not the case here.

questions.stem: In the five-sector circular flow model, the financial sector mainly:
options: channels household savings into loans for investment and consumption
collects taxes from households and businesses to fund public spending
buys Australian exports from businesses on behalf of overseas buyers
produces goods and services for households in return for spending
questions.explanation: Banks and other financial institutions take in saving, a leakage, and lend it to businesses and households, returning it to the flow as investment and spending. Collecting taxes is the government sector's role.

questions.stem: Overseas incomes fall, cutting demand for Australian exports, while Australian households save a larger share of their income. In the five-sector model:
options: an injection rises and a leakage falls, so economic activity speeds up
two leakages rise, so activity slows but national income rises
two injections fall, so economic activity slows across the economy
an injection falls and a leakage rises, so economic activity slows
questions.explanation: Exports are an injection, and saving is a leakage, so lower exports and higher saving both reduce spending on Australian production. Saving is a leakage, not an injection, so it is wrong to describe both changes as injections falling.

questions.stem: The business cycle refers to:
options: the life cycle of a single business from start-up to closure
the movement of goods from producers to consumers
the yearly pattern of retail sales across the seasons
fluctuations in the level of economic activity over time
questions.explanation: The business cycle is the pattern of expansion and contraction in economic activity, measured by changes in real GDP. Seasonal patterns repeat every year, while business cycles are irregular in length.

questions.stem: At the trough of the business cycle, the economy is most likely to have:
options: high economic activity, low unemployment and high inflation
low economic activity, low unemployment and high inflation
high economic activity, high unemployment and low inflation
low economic activity, high unemployment and low inflation
questions.explanation: The trough is the lowest point of activity, where spare capacity and job losses keep unemployment high and price pressures weak. High activity with low unemployment and rising inflation describes the peak.

questions.stem: A recession is commonly defined as:
options: any quarter in which real GDP growth slows down
any year in which inflation is above 5 per cent
two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth
two consecutive quarters of a rising unemployment rate
questions.explanation: The common, or technical, definition of a recession is real GDP falling for two quarters in a row. Slower growth means output is still rising, so it is not a recession.

questions.stem: Real GDP growth for four quarters is 0.8%, 0.3%, −0.2% and −0.4%. Which statement is correct?
options: the economy reached the trough of its cycle in the first of the four quarters
the economy met the technical definition of a recession in the last two quarters
the economy was in recession from the second quarter, when growth slowed
real GDP fell in all four quarters, so economic activity fell throughout
questions.explanation: Real GDP fell in the third and fourth quarters, giving two consecutive quarters of negative growth. In the second quarter growth slowed to 0.3% but output still rose, so the economy was not yet in recession.

questions.stem: Real GDP growth slows from 3% to 1% over a year. This means that real GDP:
options: fell by 2 per cent over the course of the year
fell, as the economy entered a recession
stayed at the same level as the year before
still rose, but at a slower rate than before
questions.explanation: A growth rate of 1% means output is still 1% higher than a year earlier; only its rate of increase has slowed. Real GDP falls only when the growth rate is negative.

questions.stem: A leading economic indicator is one that:
options: changes after the economy has already changed direction
changes at the same time as the economy changes direction
measures the level of economic activity in a past year
changes before the economy as a whole changes direction
questions.explanation: Leading indicators, such as building approvals and consumer sentiment, tend to turn before overall activity does, so they help forecast the business cycle. Indicators that change afterwards are lagging, and those that move with activity are coincident.

questions.stem: Which is generally regarded as a leading indicator?
options: the number of residential building approvals
the unemployment rate
the annual inflation rate
real gross domestic product
questions.explanation: Building approvals come before construction starts, so they signal future activity. The unemployment rate and inflation usually change after activity does, making them lagging indicators, and real GDP is coincident.

questions.stem: The unemployment rate is usually classed as a lagging indicator because:
options: firms wait until a change in demand looks lasting before hiring or firing
unemployment figures are published by the ABS only once in every five years
unemployment always rises well before economic activity begins to slow
the unemployment rate measures household spending rather than jobs
questions.explanation: Hiring and firing are costly, so businesses first adjust hours and stock, and only change staff numbers once they are confident a change in demand will last. The ABS publishes labour force data monthly, so the lag is in firms' behaviour, not in the data.

questions.stem: Building approvals and consumer sentiment have fallen for several months, while real GDP is still growing and unemployment is low. An economist would most likely forecast that:
options: economic activity will speed up, as real GDP is still growing strongly
unemployment will fall further, as unemployment is a leading indicator
the economy is already in recession, as building approvals have fallen
economic activity may slow in coming months, with unemployment rising later
questions.explanation: Falling leading indicators suggest activity will slow; GDP, a coincident indicator, has not yet turned, and unemployment, a lagging indicator, would rise last. A fall in approvals alone does not mean a recession, which requires real GDP to fall.

questions.stem: Aggregate demand is:
options: total spending by households alone on goods and services over a period
total income earned by Australians from overseas sources over a period
total spending on Australia's goods and services by all sectors over a period
total production of goods and services in Australia over a period
questions.explanation: Aggregate demand is the total spending on domestically produced goods and services by households, businesses, government and the overseas sector. Total production is aggregate supply, and household spending is only one component, consumption.

questions.stem: The components of aggregate demand are:
options: C + I + G + (X − M)
C + S + T + M
C + I + G + (M − X)
S + I + G + X
questions.explanation: Aggregate demand is consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports, exports minus imports. Imports are subtracted, not added, because they are spending on goods produced overseas.

questions.stem: Why are imports subtracted when calculating aggregate demand?
options: they are spending on goods produced overseas, not on Australian production
they reduce the revenue the government collects from taxes on trade
they are paid for with money that Australians borrow from overseas
they always cost more than goods that are produced in Australia
questions.explanation: Consumption, investment and government spending include spending on imported goods, so imports are subtracted to leave only spending on Australian production. Imports are a leakage from the circular flow of income.

questions.stem: A fall in interest rates is most likely to raise aggregate demand by:
options: raising returns on savings, encouraging households to save much more
raising the cost of imports, encouraging local spending instead
lowering tax rates, raising the disposable income of households
lowering borrowing costs, encouraging consumption and investment
questions.explanation: Cheaper credit makes it easier for households to borrow for homes and cars and for firms to borrow for new capital, so C and I rise. Lower interest rates reduce the return on saving, which encourages spending rather than saving.

questions.stem: The Australian dollar depreciates sharply against other currencies. The most likely effect on aggregate demand is:
options: a rise, as imports become cheaper for Australian households to buy
a fall, as overseas tourists now find Australia more expensive
a rise, as exports become cheaper overseas and imports dearer here
a fall, as exports become dearer overseas and imports cheaper here
questions.explanation: A lower dollar makes Australian goods cheaper for foreign buyers and imports dearer for Australians, so net exports rise. Depreciation makes imports more expensive, not cheaper, and makes Australia cheaper for foreign tourists.

questions.stem: Business confidence falls sharply. Which component of aggregate demand is most directly affected?
options: consumption, as businesses buy fewer goods for their staff
net exports, as businesses decide to export more goods
investment, as firms delay buying new capital equipment
government spending, as the government's budget shrinks
questions.explanation: Investment depends heavily on firms' expectations of future sales, so falling confidence leads them to postpone spending on capital. Consumption is spending by households, not purchases by businesses.

questions.stem: Which combination is most likely to cause a fall in aggregate demand?
options: rising interest rates and falling consumer confidence
falling interest rates and rising consumer confidence
rising overseas incomes and a depreciating dollar
higher government spending and lower income tax
questions.explanation: Higher interest rates discourage borrowing and spending, and lower confidence makes households cautious, so consumption and investment both fall. Rising overseas incomes and a weaker dollar both raise exports, increasing aggregate demand.

questions.stem: Aggregate supply refers to:
options: the total value of goods and services that are sold to other countries
the total production of goods and services in the economy over a period
the total spending on goods and services by all four sectors of the economy
the total supply of money held by banks and households in the economy
questions.explanation: Aggregate supply is the total output of goods and services produced in the economy. Total spending by all sectors is aggregate demand, and goods sold overseas are only the export part of it.

questions.stem: Which change is most likely to increase aggregate supply?
options: a drought that reduces farm output across several states
a rise in wages that is faster than growth in productivity
an improvement in labour productivity from better training
a sharp rise in the world price of oil used by industry
questions.explanation: Higher productivity means more output from the same inputs, lowering unit costs and raising the economy's productive capacity. A dearer oil price, a drought and wages outpacing productivity all raise costs or cut output, reducing aggregate supply.

questions.stem: Floods damage major rail lines and coal mines in Queensland for several months. The most likely effect is:
options: a rise in aggregate supply, as rebuilding damaged rail lines lifts output
a fall in aggregate demand, as households across Australia save more
a rise in aggregate supply, as world coal prices rise after the floods
a fall in aggregate supply, lowering output and pushing up some prices
questions.explanation: Damaged mines and rail lines cut the economy's capacity to produce and transport goods, reducing aggregate supply, lowering output and pushing up prices of goods in short supply. Rebuilding adds to spending later, but it cannot offset the lost capacity while the damage lasts.

questions.stem: Which event affects aggregate supply rather than aggregate demand?
options: an increase in government spending on public hospitals
a fall in the cost of imported components used by manufacturers
a cut in income tax rates for low- and middle-income households
a rise in consumer confidence after a strong jobs report
questions.explanation: Cheaper inputs lower firms' costs of production, so they can produce more at each price level, an increase in aggregate supply. Tax cuts, confidence and government spending all change total spending, which is aggregate demand.

questions.stem: Economic growth is measured by:
options: the change in the size of the population
the percentage change in real GDP over a period
the percentage change in nominal GDP over a period
the total value of exports over a period
questions.explanation: Economic growth is the rate at which real GDP, the volume of output, increases. Nominal GDP can rise simply because prices rise, without any extra output.

questions.stem: Why do economists use real rather than nominal GDP to measure economic growth?
options: real GDP includes the value of unpaid work such as caring and volunteering
real GDP adjusts for population size, showing the output of each person
real GDP excludes government spending, showing only private economic activity
real GDP removes the effect of price changes, showing the change in output
questions.explanation: Real GDP is adjusted for inflation, so its change reflects a change in the quantity of goods and services produced. Adjusting for population gives real GDP per capita, a separate measure.

questions.stem: Real GDP rises from $2,000 billion to $2,050 billion over a year. The rate of economic growth is:
questions.explanation: Growth is the change divided by the starting value: $50 billion ÷ $2,000 billion × 100 = 2.5%. Dividing by the final value of $2,050 billion gives 2.44%, which uses the wrong base.

questions.stem: Nominal GDP grows by 6% in a year, while the general price level rises by 4%. Real GDP growth is approximately:
questions.explanation: Real growth is approximately nominal growth minus inflation: 6% − 4% = 2%. Adding the two rates would treat price rises as extra output, which is the error real GDP is designed to remove.

questions.stem: Real GDP grows by 2% in a year while the population grows by 2.5%. Real GDP per capita:
options: stays the same, as total output grew
falls by about 0.5%
rises by about 0.5%
rises by about 4.5%
questions.explanation: Real GDP per capita changes by roughly the growth in real GDP minus population growth: 2% − 2.5% ≈ −0.5%. Total output grew, but it is shared among people faster than it grew, so output per person fell.

questions.stem: Which is a potential benefit of economic growth for living standards?
options: a more equal distribution of income across the economy in every case
less traffic congestion as more goods and services are being produced
more jobs and higher incomes, with more tax revenue for public services
less pollution in cities as the economy produces more goods and services
questions.explanation: Growth creates jobs, raises incomes and lifts tax revenue that can fund health and education. More production tends to add to pollution and congestion rather than reduce them, which is why these are listed among the costs of growth.

questions.stem: 'Affluenza' refers to:
options: the movement of wealthy residents out of crowded cities to regional areas
stress, debt and dissatisfaction that come from pursuing ever more possessions
the spread of wealth from high-income households to low-income households
rising prices caused by too much spending during a boom in the economy
questions.explanation: Affluenza describes the harm to wellbeing from overwork, overconsumption and debt in the pursuit of more material goods. It is a non-material cost of growth, not a description of inflation in a boom.

questions.stem: Why can very rapid economic growth lead to 'boom and bust' cycles?
options: rapid growth always lowers the inflation rate, and this then reduces total spending
rapid growth reduces employment across the economy, causing output to fall later
rapid growth reduces the level of imports, which harms Australia's trading partners
spending outpaces productive capacity, raising inflation and later forcing a sharp slowdown
questions.explanation: When spending grows faster than the economy can produce, prices and asset values rise unsustainably and debt builds up, until spending collapses into a downturn. Rapid growth tends to raise inflation rather than lower it.

questions.stem: One potential cost of economic growth is widening inequality. This can occur when:
options: growth raises the incomes of all households by exactly the same percentage
growth lowers the prices of the goods most often bought by low-income households
growth reduces the number of jobs available to the most highly skilled workers
the gains from growth go mainly to those who own assets or have in-demand skills
questions.explanation: If asset owners and highly skilled workers capture most of the extra income, the gap between high- and low-income households grows. Equal percentage rises would leave relative shares unchanged.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of using real GDP per capita to measure living standards?
options: it does not adjust for changes in the general price level
it counts only government spending, not private spending
it does not show how income is distributed among people
it does not adjust for changes in the size of the population
questions.explanation: Real GDP per capita is an average, so it can rise while many people's incomes stagnate. It does adjust for prices, because it is real, and for population, because it is per capita.

questions.stem: After a bushfire, spending on rebuilding homes raises real GDP. This shows that GDP:
options: can rise even when wellbeing falls, as it counts spending on repairing damage
always falls after a natural disaster, because production capacity is destroyed
measures non-material living standards as well as material living standards
excludes all spending that replaces goods and buildings that already existed
questions.explanation: GDP counts the value of rebuilding as new production, but people are no better off than before the fire, and they have suffered losses GDP does not record. GDP measures market output, not wellbeing, which is why it can mislead about living standards.

questions.stem: The Human Development Index combines measures of:
options: health, employment and the quality of housing
education, pollution and crime rates
health, education and standard of living
income, wealth and the inflation rate
questions.explanation: The HDI combines life expectancy at birth, years of schooling and income per person, so it reflects some non-material living standards as well as material ones. It does not include pollution, crime or housing.

questions.stem: The Genuine Progress Indicator differs from GDP mainly because it:
options: is calculated using nominal values rather than real values
counts only those goods that are traded across national borders
subtracts costs such as pollution and adds the value of unpaid work
measures only the output produced by the government sector
questions.explanation: The GPI starts from personal consumption, then adjusts it, deducting costs such as pollution and crime and adding benefits GDP misses, such as volunteering and household work. This makes it a broader measure of progress than market output alone.

questions.stem: Two countries have the same income per person, but Country X has higher life expectancy and more years of schooling than Country Y. Compared with Country Y, Country X would have:
options: the same HDI, because their incomes per person are identical
a lower HDI, because spending more on health reduces income
a higher real GDP growth rate, because health raises output
a higher HDI, reflecting better non-material living standards
questions.explanation: The HDI includes health and education as well as income, so X's better health and schooling raise its score even though incomes are equal. Equal incomes give equal scores only on that one component, not on the whole index.

questions.stem: The OECD Better Life Index is a useful alternative to GDP because it:
options: ranks countries by their total real GDP and the size of their populations
is calculated by each country's own government using its own chosen methods
lets users weight dimensions such as health, housing and environment by what they value
measures only the income and wealth of the households within each country
questions.explanation: The index covers eleven dimensions of wellbeing, including material and non-material ones, and lets users weight them by importance. Measuring only income and wealth would repeat the narrow view that alternatives to GDP are designed to widen.
